subsection: 5. Contemporary initiatives to improve access to education

notes.h: Routes into third-level education (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Access routes let students who would be disadvantaged by the normal points system enter third-level courses.
points: HEAR (Higher Education Access Route) lets students from socially disadvantaged backgrounds who meet set criteria enter third-level courses on reduced points.
Students admitted through HEAR receive support services in college once they have started their course.
DARE (Disability Access Route to Education) lets students with a disability, such as dyslexia, autism or a sensory impairment, enter third-level courses on reduced points.
Students admitted through DARE receive ongoing support in college, such as assistive technology and exam accommodations.
Post Leaving Certificate courses and Level 7 courses provide an alternative route into higher education for students who did not progress directly from second level.
Springboard offers free part-time higher education courses to job seekers, aimed at improving their employability.

notes.h: Retention and inclusion in second-level schools (Higher Level only)
points: DEIS (Delivering Equality of Opportunity in Schools) is an action plan for schools in disadvantaged areas, with extra staffing, homework clubs, after-school supports and mentoring programmes.
Under DEIS, schools may provide a school meals programme and access to home school community liaison services.
The School Completion Programme aims to reduce the number of students leaving school early and to ease the transfer from primary to second level.
The Home School Community Liaison (HSCL) scheme links schools with parents and the community, and identifies students who need financial or learning support.
The Junior Cycle Support Programme (JCSP) targets students most at risk of leaving school early, and it certifies the skills they attain and the subject statements they complete.
The National Behaviour Support Service (NBSS) helps students at risk of exclusion because of behavioural problems, through counselling and anger management programmes.

notes.h: Second-chance and adult access initiatives (Higher Level only)
points: Youthreach is a two-year integrated training and education programme for young people aged 15 to 20 who left school without qualifications, and participants receive a training allowance.
Youthreach centres are located throughout the country, including traveller training centres and community training workshops.
VTOS (Vocational Training Opportunities Scheme) offers courses designed to meet the educational needs of unemployed people over 21, with training allowances similar to social welfare entitlements.
The Back to Education Allowance (BTEA) helps people on social welfare payments to attend approved full-time or part-time education courses.
Community Education schemes provide adult literacy and other community-based courses in local settings.
Aontas, the Irish National Association of Adult Education, promotes the development of adult learning and gives advice and support across adult education.

keyTerms.definition: The Higher Education Access Route, which admits students from socially disadvantaged backgrounds to third-level courses on reduced points.
The Disability Access Route to Education, which admits students with a disability to third-level courses on reduced points and provides ongoing support.
Delivering Equality of Opportunity in Schools, an action plan that gives extra supports to schools in disadvantaged areas.
A programme that aims to keep young people in school and reduce early school leaving.
A scheme that links schools with parents and the wider community to support pupils, particularly those who need extra help.
A two-year integrated training and education programme for young people who left school without qualifications.
The Vocational Training Opportunities Scheme, which provides courses for unemployed people over 21.
A social welfare-linked support that helps people on payments to attend approved education courses.
A process that lets applicants enter a course on reduced points or through an alternative assessment, usually because of disadvantage or disability.
The Irish National Association of Adult Education, which promotes and supports adult learning.

questions.prompt: Outline the purpose of the HEAR scheme.
questions.model: Any three, two marks each: it admits students from socially disadvantaged backgrounds who meet set criteria; entry is on reduced points; it widens participation in third-level education; students receive support services in college after they start.

questions.prompt: Discuss two contemporary initiatives that improve access to education for students at risk of educational disadvantage.
questions.model: Each initiative needs its name, its aim, how it works and an evaluation of its effect. Option one, HEAR: reduced-points entry for students from socially disadvantaged backgrounds, with college support; limited to students who meet the criteria, so it helps only some students who are disadvantaged. Option two, DEIS: an action plan for schools in disadvantaged areas with extra staffing, homework clubs, after-school supports, mentoring and school meals; evaluated by its focus on whole-school resources and by the risk that it does not reach students in non-DEIS schools. Other accepted options include the School Completion Programme, the Junior Cycle Support Programme, Youthreach, VTOS and the Home School Community Liaison scheme, each with its target group and a comment on its strengths and limitations.
